```text
[  354.730563][ T3615] veth425341f: entered promiscuous mode
[  354.897404][ T3615] eth0: renamed from veth7c6048a
[  354.910544][   T75] br-76627188d0fc: port 2(veth425341f) entered blocking state
[  354.916695][   T75] br-76627188d0fc: port 2(veth425341f) entered forwarding state
```

These messages look consistent with containers being repeatedly created/stopped/recreated during the failed startup path, rather than a standalone host networking issue.

这些日志看起来更像是失败启动路径中容器被反复创建、停止、重建时产生的现象，而不是独立的宿主机网络问题。

The release currently has several short cold-start budgets, for example:

当前 release 中多个首次启动等待时间偏短，例如：

```text
deploy/one-click/scripts/systemd/mysql-postcheck.sh:
wait_for_container_health "${CUBE_SANDBOX_MYSQL_CONTAINER:-cube-sandbox-mysql}" 40 2

deploy/one-click/systemd/cube-sandbox-mysql.service:
TimeoutStartSec=180s

deploy/one-click/scripts/systemd/coredns-postcheck.sh:
wait_for_udp_port "${COREDNS_BIND_ADDR}" 53 30 1

deploy/one-click/systemd/cube-sandbox-coredns.service:
TimeoutStartSec=60s

deploy/one-click/scripts/systemd/cubemaster-postcheck.sh:
wait_for_http "http://${CUBEMASTER_ADDR:-127.0.0.1:8089}/notify/health" 30 1

deploy/one-click/systemd/cube-sandbox-cubemaster.service:
TimeoutStartSec=60s

deploy/one-click/scripts/systemd/redis-postcheck.sh:
wait_for_container_health "${CUBE_SANDBOX_REDIS_CONTAINER:-cube-sandbox-redis}" 40 2

deploy/one-click/systemd/cube-sandbox-redis.service:
TimeoutStartSec=60s
```

## Workaround that made the install succeed

The workaround that made the same clean VM install successfully was to patch the downloaded one-click bundle before it starts the systemd target.

让同一个全新 VM 安装成功的 workaround，是在 one-click 下载并解压 release bundle 之后、真正启动 systemd target 之前修改已解压出来的安装脚本。

The important insertion point is inside the downloaded bundle’s `install.sh`, after `install_systemd_units` has installed the unit files and before `start_systemd_target` starts `cube-sandbox-control.target`.

关键插入点是在下载解压出来的 `${BUNDLE_DIR}/install.sh` 里，`install_systemd_units` 已经安装 unit 文件之后、`start_systemd_target` 启动 `cube-sandbox-control.target` 之前。

Practically, this was done by modifying the wrapper `online-install.sh` flow to insert the following block before the line matching `^start_systemd_target$` in `${BUNDLE_DIR}/install.sh`:

实际操作上，是在 `online-install.sh` 流程里，对 `${BUNDLE_DIR}/install.sh` 做一次 `sed` 注入，把下面这段插到匹配 `^start_systemd_target$` 的行之前：

```bash
sed -i "/^start_systemd_target$/i\\
echo \"[one-click] Extending cold-start timeouts for MySQL/CoreDNS/CubeMaster\"\\
sed -i -E '/wait_for_container_health .*cube-sandbox-mysql/ s/[0-9]+ 2/240 2/' /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/scripts/systemd/mysql-postcheck.sh\\
sed -i -E '/wait_for_udp_port .*COREDNS_BIND_ADDR/ s/53 [0-9]+ 1/53 300 1/' /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/scripts/systemd/coredns-postcheck.sh\\
sed -i -E '/wait_for_http .*8089/ s/[0-9]+ 1/300 1/' /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/scripts/systemd/cubemaster-postcheck.sh\\
grep -q '240 2' /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/scripts/systemd/mysql-postcheck.sh\\
grep -q '53 300 1' /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/scripts/systemd/coredns-postcheck.sh\\
grep -q '300 1' /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/scripts/systemd/cubemaster-postcheck.sh\\
install -d -m 0755 /etc/systemd/system/cube-sandbox-mysql.service.d\\
install -d -m 0755 /etc/systemd/system/cube-sandbox-coredns.service.d\\
install -d -m 0755 /etc/systemd/system/cube-sandbox-cubemaster.service.d\\
{ echo \"[Service]\"; echo \"TimeoutStartSec=900s\"; } > /etc/systemd/system/cube-sandbox-mysql.service.d/timeout.conf\\
{ echo \"[Service]\"; echo \"TimeoutStartSec=900s\"; } > /etc/systemd/system/cube-sandbox-coredns.service.d/timeout.conf\\
{ echo \"[Service]\"; echo \"TimeoutStartSec=900s\"; } > /etc/systemd/system/cube-sandbox-cubemaster.service.d/timeout.conf\\
systemctl daemon-reload\\
" "${BUNDLE_DIR}/install.sh"
```

This modifies the following VM-side files after the bundle has been installed under `/usr/local/services/cubetoolbox`, but before the services are started:

这会在 bundle 安装到 `/usr/local/services/cubetoolbox` 之后、服务启动之前，修改 VM 内的这些文件：

```text
/usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/scripts/systemd/mysql-postcheck.sh
/usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/scripts/systemd/coredns-postcheck.sh
/usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/scripts/systemd/cubemaster-postcheck.sh

/etc/systemd/system/cube-sandbox-mysql.service.d/timeout.conf
/etc/systemd/system/cube-sandbox-coredns.service.d/timeout.conf
/etc/systemd/system/cube-sandbox-cubemaster.service.d/timeout.conf
```

After this change, the effective settings became:

修改后，实际生效的配置为：

```text
cube-sandbox-mysql.service:
TimeoutStartUSec=15min
DropInPaths=/etc/systemd/system/cube-sandbox-mysql.service.d/timeout.conf

cube-sandbox-coredns.service:
TimeoutStartUSec=15min
DropInPaths=/etc/systemd/system/cube-sandbox-coredns.service.d/timeout.conf

cube-sandbox-cubemaster.service:
TimeoutStartUSec=15min
DropInPaths=/etc/systemd/system/cube-sandbox-cubemaster.service.d/timeout.conf
```

And the patched postcheck scripts contained:

对应的 postcheck 脚本变成：

```text
/usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/scripts/systemd/mysql-postcheck.sh:
wait_for_container_health "${CUBE_SANDBOX_MYSQL_CONTAINER:-cube-sandbox-mysql}" 240 2 || die "mysql container not ready"

/usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/scripts/systemd/coredns-postcheck.sh:
wait_for_udp_port "${COREDNS_BIND_ADDR}" 53 300 1 || die "coredns udp port not ready"

/usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/scripts/systemd/cubemaster-postcheck.sh:
wait_for_http "http://${CUBEMASTER_ADDR:-127.0.0.1:8089}/notify/health" 300 1 || die "cubemaster health not ready"
```

With these changes, the same environment completed successfully:

使用这些修改后，同一环境安装成功：

```text
[quickcheck] check systemd units
[quickcheck] check container runtime state
[quickcheck] 1/5 check network-agent healthz
[quickcheck] 2/5 check network-agent readyz
[quickcheck] 3/5 check cubemaster /notify/health
[quickcheck] 4/5 check cube-api /health
[quickcheck] 5/5 check essential sockets and config
[quickcheck] OK
[one-click] install complete (role=control)
```

## Additional Context

This appears to be a timeout-budget problem rather than a permanent service failure. On first boot, MySQL initialization and CubeMaster migrations can take longer than the current postcheck/systemd budgets. Once an early service is killed or restarted by systemd, downstream services such as DNS, CubeMaster, Cube API, WebUI, cube-proxy, or cube-egress may surface the failure later.

这个问题看起来不是服务本身永久失败，而是首次冷启动 timeout budget 不够。首次启动时，MySQL 初始化和 CubeMaster migration 可能超过当前 postcheck/systemd 等待时间。一旦上游服务被 systemd 超时杀掉或重启，下游 DNS、CubeMaster、Cube API、WebUI、cube-proxy、cube-egress 等服务会以不同形式暴露失败。

Another important observation is that once the MySQL container is interrupted during its first initialization, simply increasing the timeout and retrying may still fail. The named Docker volume used by MySQL can be left in a partially initialized or corrupted state, so later retries may keep failing until the MySQL container and its volume are removed.

另一个重要现象是：如果 MySQL 容器在首次初始化过程中被超时中断，后续仅仅提高 timeout 后重试可能仍然失败。MySQL 使用的 Docker named volume 可能已经处于半初始化或损坏状态，因此之后的重试会持续失败，直到删除 MySQL 容器和对应 volume。

In this environment, recovery required removing the MySQL container and volume before retrying the installation/startup path, for example:

在这个环境中，恢复时需要先删除 MySQL 容器和 volume，再重新尝试安装/启动流程，例如：

```bash
docker rm -f cube-sandbox-mysql
docker volume rm support_cube-sandbox-mysql-data
```

title: feat(web): add interactive sandbox terminal
body:
## Problem

CubeSandbox supports non-interactive command execution, but the WebUI could not
open an interactive shell in a running sandbox. Closes #643.

## Solution (reworked per review)

Following @fslongjin's review, the terminal is now an **operational capability
implemented entirely in CubeOps** — no new RPC, and **no CubeAPI changes**.

CubeOps bridges the browser WebSocket straight to the sandbox's in-guest
**envd** `process.Process` PTY API (`Start` / `SendInput` / `Update` /
`SendSignal`) — the same envd path CubeOps already uses for command execution
(there is even a ready client in `sdk/go/pty.go`).

```text
WebUI / xterm.js
      │  authenticated WebSocket ( /opsapi/v1/sdk/sandboxes/<id>/terminal/ws )
      ▼
CubeOps  (JWT auth · audit · session limit · frame/idle limits)
      │  envd Connect stream ( process.Process )
      ▼
envd (in-guest) → PTY → workload shell
```

## What changed vs the first revision

- **Removed** (reverted to upstream): CubeAPI WebSocket proxy + config/state/
  routes, the CubeMaster WebSocket gateway + `TERMINAL_GATEWAY_TOKEN`, the
  Cubelet `AttachTerminal` streaming RPC (+ proto / `pb.go` regen), and the
  CubeShim PTY-resize change.
- **Added** (CubeOps): `internal/service/terminal.go` (envd PTY client) and
  `internal/handler/terminal.go` (WebSocket handler), registered at
  `/api/v1/sdk/sandboxes/:id/terminal/ws`.
- **WebUI**: the xterm.js dialog now targets CubeOps and consumes raw PTY output
  as binary frames; the multi-container picker is dropped (the envd PTY is
  sandbox-scoped).
- **Deploy/docs**: the `/opsapi/` WebSocket upgrade is forwarded in the bundled
  nginx / Helm / Terraform configs; `docs/web-terminal.md` rewritten.

## Security & lifecycle

- The CubeOps JWT rides in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` (never in the URL); an
  unauthenticated dial is rejected with **401 before upgrade**. Because the JWT
  is unreachable cross-origin, this also defeats cross-site WebSocket hijacking,
  so `Origin` is not used as a second boundary.
- Per-sandbox session limit (4 → HTTP 429), 64 KiB frame cap, 30-minute idle
  timeout.
- Paired `terminal.session.open` / `terminal.session.close` audit records with
  the operator (from the JWT) and sandbox ID.
- On disconnect the PTY is `SIGKILL`ed so it cannot block the sandbox.

## Verification

Validated on a live single-node PVM host:

- CubeOps `go build ./...`, `go vet`, and unit tests (Connect framing,
  subprotocol parsing, dimension clamp, session limiter) pass.
- **End-to-end through the CubeOps WebSocket handler into a real MicroVM**:
  unauthenticated dial → `401`; authenticated dial negotiates `cube-terminal`;
  `id` → `uid=0(root)`, `uname -sm` → `Linux x86_64`; `resize` reflected in
  `stty size` (24×80 → 50×132); clean exit with `{"type":"exit"}`; paired
  open/close audit emitted.
- WebUI `tsc` type-check and `vite build` pass.

## Open questions for the maintainer

1. **Multi-container selection** was dropped because the envd PTY is
   sandbox-scoped. Happy to map it to an `exec`-into-container instead if you'd
   prefer to keep that.
2. This assumes running sandboxes always have envd reachable — the same
   assumption CubeOps' existing envd command path already relies on.

title: refactor(cubemaster): migrate HTTP API from gorilla/mux to gin-gonic/gin
body:
## What this PR does

Migrate CubeMaster's HTTP API from `gorilla/mux` to `gin-gonic/gin`. This is a **router-layer + handler-layer** migration (not a thin adapter): the giant `cube.HttpHandler` / `inner.HttpHandler` / `notify.HttpHandler` switch dispatchers are replaced by gin's radix-tree routing, and the handlers are native `gin.HandlerFunc`s.

### Router layer
- `gorilla/mux` → `gin-gonic/gin` (release mode). Routes registered directly via `RegisterCubeRoutes` / `RegisterInnerRoutes` / `RegisterNotifyRoutes` / `RegisterMetaRoutes`.
- Request middleware (logging / auth / recovery / trace) mounted on a root group so **matched routes** keep it, while **NoRoute / NoMethod stay bare** — gorilla/mux does not run router middleware on unmatched/method-mismatch requests, so neither does this (probes/mistyped URLs don't enter `checkAuth`).

### Handler layer
- All handlers are `func(c *gin.Context)`, reading path params via `c.Param` (build_id / snapshot_id / operation_id / sandbox_id / filename) — the manual path-parsing helpers are gone.
- **Standardized response writes**: success-path responses in cube/inner/notify go through `common.WriteAPI` / `common.WriteListAPI` (HTTP 200 + the JSON envelope serialized via **FastestJsoniter**, not gin's `encoding/json`), so no handler hand-rolls `c.Writer` + Content-Type. The `meta` package keeps its own error writer for its intentional HTTP-400 paths (malformed request body), which intentionally differ from the cube contract (HTTP 200 + ret_code); `common.WriteErr` is a convenience error-envelope helper currently exercised by the common package's contract tests rather than the hot path.

### Backward compatibility (preserved + tested)
- Response envelope `{ret:{ret_code,ret_msg},requestID}` and **HTTP 200** (errors carried in `ret_code`) — unchanged.
- **FastestJsoniter** serialization — unchanged (Content-Type is exactly `application/json`, not gin's default `application/json; charset=utf-8`).
- NoRoute → plain **HTTP 404**; method-mismatch → **HTTP 405** (empty body). gin additionally emits an RFC-7231 `Allow` header listing the allowed methods (mux's 405 did not) — intentional, locked by test.
- `POST /internal/fake_create` kept (legacy `200 + {ret_code:-1, Not Found}`).
- URL paths, auth flow, error codes — unchanged.

Two intentional deltas vs a literal mux mirror:
- `GET /cube/snapshot/storage` is registered as an explicit static route ahead of `/cube/snapshot/:snapshot_id` (safer than the old path-parse-inside-handler approach).
- gin's 405 response includes an RFC-7231 `Allow` header (mux's 405 did not).

### Tests
- Request-level contract tests: bare 404/405 body+status, middleware skipped on 404/405 (no auth), static-priority snapshot/storage, method-agnostic `/internal/{query,ws}`.
- Engine-level contract tests: `WriteAPI`/`WriteListAPI`/`WriteErr` emit HTTP 200 + `application/json` (FastestJsoniter) + the envelope; `fake_create` envelope test.
- meta/notify request-level tests (gomonkey, run with `-gcflags=all=-l`): meta `node_id` path param, labels `node_id`+`key` query, isolation PUT/DELETE, malformed register body → 400; notify `/notify/host` good/bad body, `/notify/health`. Lock the intentional notify-200-on-bad-body and meta-400+MasterInternalError contract details.
- Gin routing micro-benchmark + PVM A/B (see comments): no creation-latency regression vs mux at c=1/c=10.

Verified: `go build ./...`, `go vet`, `go test ./pkg/server/... ./pkg/service/httpservice/...`, `gofmt` all clean.

Signed-off-by: sparkzky <sparkhhhhhhhhhh@outlook.com>
Assisted-by: Orca:zai/glm-5.2

title: feat(lifecycle): deliver sandbox lifecycle events to webhook endpoints from CLM
body:
## Problem

CubeSandbox records lifecycle events internally, but external orchestration and operations systems must poll the sandbox API to detect create, pause, resume, and delete transitions. Polling adds latency and unnecessary load.

Closes #642.

## Solution

Deliver lifecycle events to external HTTP endpoints from **cube-lifecycle-manager (CLM)**, which already consumes the durable lifecycle events stream (`cube:v1:shared:sandbox:lifecycle:events`). CubeAPI stays stateless and CubeMaster needs no changes: `create`, `delete`, and `state` (paused/running) transitions are already published to the stream.

Each endpoint owns an independent Redis consumer group (`webhook:<hash>`), so a slow or unavailable receiver cannot block other subscriptions or the auto-pause/resume loop. Delivery is at-least-once: an event is acknowledged only after it reaches a terminal state (delivered, permanently rejected, or retries exhausted), and a restarted replica redelivers whatever its consumer left pending. Multiple replicas share a group and split deliveries via consumer names, matching CLM's existing HA model.

**Durability:** there is no in-memory event queue. Redis Streams is the only buffer — each endpoint's worker reads the durable stream via `XREADGROUP` and ACKs an entry only after it reaches a terminal state, so a CLM restart (including `kill -9`) redelivers whatever its consumer left pending, with the original event timestamp preserved.

## Changes

- Configure endpoints with `CUBE_LCM_WEBHOOK_ENDPOINTS` (JSON array: `url`, optional `events` filter, optional `secret`), plus `CUBE_LCM_WEBHOOK_MAX_RETRIES`, `CUBE_LCM_WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT`, `CUBE_LCM_WEBHOOK_RETRY_BASE`. URLs must be http(s) without userinfo; secrets must be at least 16 bytes; event names are validated against the four known events so a typo fails fast instead of leaving a silently dead subscription.
- Emit `sandbox.created`, `sandbox.deleted`, `sandbox.paused`, and `sandbox.resumed`; metadata `update` ops and transition markers (`pausing`/`resuming`) are never delivered.
- Payload carries `version`, `event`, `timestamp` (taken from the stream entry, so redeliveries keep the original event time), and `sandbox_id`; `sandbox.created` adds `template_id` when known, and `sandbox.paused`/`sandbox.resumed` add `state`.
- Sign the exact JSON request body with HMAC-SHA256 in `X-Cube-Signature-256` when a secret is configured.
- Retry `5xx`, `408`, and `429` responses with exponential backoff and jitter; other `4xx` responses are permanent and not retried. The whole delivery is capped at 30 seconds, and automatic redirects are disabled so a configured endpoint cannot bounce delivery to an internal service. Log lines use a sanitized endpoint label (credentials, query, and fragment stripped).
- Add a dependency-free receiver example with signature verification, replay protection, and content-type validation, plus a verification script for deployed environments.
- Document configuration, delivery semantics, and operations (`XPENDING`/`XAUTOCLAIM`) in the CLM README.

## Scope

- Subscriptions are static configuration; this PR does not add the optional REST management API discussed in #642.
- Delivery is at-least-once, so receivers must be idempotent. Entries pending on a permanently dead replica stay observable via `XPENDING` and can be reassigned with `XAUTOCLAIM`.
- At-least-once is bounded by the retry budget: once retries are exhausted the event is ACKed and dropped, so a receiver that is unavailable for longer than the budget (~2s connection-refused / ~22s hanging, at the defaults) permanently loses those transitions. A keep-pending / dead-letter mode is under discussion in review.
- Generic alerting products that require a product-specific payload (e.g. a WeCom bot expecting `msgtype`) still need an adapter in front; the receiver example shows how.

## Verification

Unit tests (Go, `httptest` + pure functions, no new dependencies):

```text
go test ./...   # cube-lifecycle-manager: all 12 packages ok
go vet ./...    # clean
```

Live end-to-end on a deployed server (Redis 7.2 + CLM + the example receiver):

- `sandbox.created` / `paused` / `resumed` / `deleted` delivered in stream order with correct payloads (`version`, `template_id`, `state`) and receiver-verified HMAC signatures; `update` ops and `pausing` markers correctly filtered out.
- Consumer-group isolation confirmed: `webhook:<hash>` is disjoint from `cube-proxy-sidecar`, and an endpoint whose receiver is down backs up only its own group.
- Crash recovery: `kill -9` mid-retry leaves the event pending; after restart CLM logs `redelivering pending events`, redelivers with the original event timestamp, and the pending list drains to zero.
- Receiver content-type handling: `application/json` accepted (parameters tolerated), others rejected with 415.

## Review

Auto-review findings addressed in-place:

- M1 (unknown event names silently accepted) — now rejected at config load, with tests.
- L1 (URL path preserved in log labels) — documented as intentional in `Label()`; secrets belong in the `secret` field, never the path.
- L2 (no content-type check in the example receiver) — returns 415 for non-JSON bodies.
- L3 (retry-delay test is a range check) — left as-is; a property-based distribution check adds little over the existing bounds test.

Assisted-by: Kimi Code CLI:K2

<details>
<summary>Implementation history</summary>

A previous iteration of this PR implemented delivery inside CubeAPI, using a bounded per-endpoint in-memory `mpsc` queue that dropped events under backpressure. It was reworked following review feedback on the issue's other PRs: CubeAPI must stay stateless, and event delivery belongs in an independent service rather than an in-process worker with in-memory queues. The current implementation is Go, under `cube-lifecycle-manager/internal/webhook/`, and buffers nothing in process.

</details>

## Summary

Replace the previous push-from-GitHub approach for syncing images to TCR CN with a dedicated `sync_cn` job that:

- Uses `crane copy` to replicate per-arch (amd64/arm64) and multi-arch manifest images from GHCR to TCR CN

- Added `sync_cn` job to `.github/workflows/release-docker-images.yml`
- Runs after `publish_manifests` succeeds and only for the `TencentCloud/CubeSandbox` repository
- Installs `crane` v0.20.3 and logs into both GHCR and TCR CN registries via secrets
- Copies all component images (per-arch + manifest tags) using `crane copy`

## Why

Pushing large container layers from GitHub-hosted US runners directly to a CN registry is slow and unreliable. Running the sync from a China-side self-hosted runner via `crane copy` (registry-to-registry) is significantly faster and more reliable.

title: fix(vmm): index snapshot pagemap by the host's real page size
body:
The snapshot dirty-page tracking hardcoded a 4 KiB page size for all pagemap and kpageflags math. On ARM64 hosts configured with 64 KiB base pages, /proc/self/pagemap and /proc/kpageflags are indexed in units of the kernel's real page size, so the hardcoded 4096 mis-indexed the pagemap and could silently corrupt snapshots.

Probe the host page size once via sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE), cache it, and expose it as a single crate-wide source of truth. All page-index, seek-offset and range-length computations across the anon, soft-dirty, and anon-intersect-soft-dirty filters now scale with this value.

Consolidate the duplicated per-page bitmap coalescing into a shared, page-size-parameterized helper so the ranges it emits scale with the injected page size. Keeping it pure lets the tests drive both the 4 KiB and 64 KiB paths without requiring a matching-page-size kernel.

title: [Feature Request] Python SDK Support for Volume Feature (Volume CRUD + volumeMounts)

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
## Background

CubeSandbox has implemented a complete Volume plugin framework on the server side, providing persistent storage across sandbox lifecycles with e2b Volume API compatibility.

The following capabilities are already supported on the server side:
- ✅ Volume CRUD API (e2b compatible)
- ✅ Sandbox mounting via `volumeMounts`
- ✅ Controller / Node Hook abstraction protocol
- ✅ Cross-node reference counting

However, **the Python SDK does not yet expose Volume-related functionality**. Developers currently have to call the raw HTTP API directly, which is error-prone and lacks the ergonomics expected from an SDK.

---

## Feature Request

Please add full Volume support to the Python SDK, covering the following:

### 1. Volume CRUD

```python
from cubesandbox import CubeSandbox

client = CubeSandbox(api_key="...")

# Create a volume
volume = client.volumes.create(name="my-data", driver="cos")
print(volume.
volume_id, volume.token)

# List all volumes
volumes = client.volumes.list()

# Get a specific volume
volume = client.volumes.get(volume_id="my-data")

# Delete a volume (all sandboxes using it must be destroyed first)
client.volumes.delete(volume_id="my-data")
```

### 2. Mount a Volume When Creating a Sandbox

```python
from cubesandbox import VolumeMount

sandbox = client.sandbox.create(
    template_id="base",
    volume_mounts=[
        VolumeMount(name="my-data", path="/workspace")
    ]
)
```

### 3. Data Models

Suggested new types (dataclass or Pydantic model):

```python
@dataclass
class Volume:
    volume_id: str
    name: str
    token: str = ""

@dataclass
class VolumeMount:
    name: str   # must match an existing volume_id
    path: str   # mount path inside the sandbox
```

```python
try:
client.volumes.delete(volume_id="my-data")
except VolumeInUseError as e:
    print(f"Cannot delete volume while it is still mounted: {e}")
```
---

## Goals
Enable Python SDK users to manage persistent Volumes and mount them into sandboxes through a clean, idiomatic API — without having to call raw HTTP endpoints directly. This brings the Python SDK to feature parity with the server-side Volume plugin framework and makes CubeSandbox's persistent storage story accessible to Python developers out of the box.

title: fix(agent): show friendly error message when container creation fails
body:
## Problem

When a user creates a template from a custom image that is missing required files (e.g. envd), container creation fails during mount propagation. The error message returned to the user is unhelpful — a bare exit code with no indication of what actually went wrong:

```
500: CubeMaster returned error code -1: failed to run container <id>:
  failed to create shim task: Others("...Exec mount failed:exec process
  exit code:1\n\nStack backtrace:...")
```

## Root Cause

`start_exec_process` in the agent spawns a child process (the agent binary re-executed with the `exec` subcommand) to perform mount propagation. When the child fails, it calls `exit_proc_failed()` which prints the real error reason (e.g. `"the source dir X not exists"`) and exits with code 1.

However, the parent process (`start_exec_process`) never captured the childs stdout/stderr — it only called `child.wait()` and checked the exit code. The real error message was printed to inherited stdout and lost; the parent returned only `"exec process exit code:1"`.

## Fix (2 files, +34/-8)

**`agent/rustjail/src/container.rs`** — `start_exec_process`:
- Add `.stdout(Stdio::piped()).stderr(Stdio::piped())` to the child Command
- Replace `child.wait()` with `child.wait_with_output()` which atomically waits and drains both pipes (also eliminates a potential pipe-buffer deadlock when the child output exceeds 64 KB)
- On failure (exit code ≠ 0), surface the childs stderr (preferred) or stdout as the error message instead of a bare exit code
- On success, log captured stdout via `slog::debug` to preserve observability

**`agent/cube/src/rootfs.rs`** — `exit_proc_failed`:
- Change `println!` to `eprintln!` so error messages go to stderr, cleanly separated from informational stdout output

## Test Results

### Environment
- CubeSandbox cluster deployed via PVM (single node)
- Fixed agent binary built with `cargo build --release` and injected into the guest image (`/sbin/init`)
- `busybox:latest` (from Tencent Cloud mirror) used as a minimal image that lacks envd and required mount sources

### Test 1: Regression check — normal sandbox creation
Created a sandbox from an existing READY template (`sandbox-code:latest`).

**Result: ✅ SUCCESS** — the fixed agent does not break normal operation.

### Test 2: Error scenario — sandbox from minimal image
1. Created a template from `busybox:latest` → **READY** (template `tpl-36d23022af304330bb7b6d74`)
2. Created a sandbox from the busybox template → triggers snapshot restore path → `start_exec_process` → mount propagation failure

**Error message comparison:**

| | Error Message |
|---|---|
| **Before fix** | `Exec mount failed:exec process exit code:1` |
| **After fix** | `Exec mount failed:open /proc/73/ns/mnt failed:No such file or directory (os error 2)` |

The user now sees the **specific failure reason** instead of a meaningless exit code.

title: [codex] Add interactive WebUI terminal access
body:
## Summary

- add an xterm.js terminal dialog to the sandbox list and detail views, including multi-container selection, resize, clipboard, fullscreen, disconnect, and reconnect controls
- add authenticated CubeAPI terminal session creation with 60-second one-time grants, a same-origin WebSocket bridge, configurable idle timeout, target validation, and structured audit events
- add the CubeMaster WebSocket relay and Cubelet bidirectional gRPC TTY implementation backed by containerd `task.Exec`
- forward containerd PTY resize requests through CubeShim to the guest agent
- update OpenAPI/generated types, MSW mocks, English/Chinese i18n, tests, and WebUI documentation

## Why

Running sandboxes previously supported only detached execution with dummy I/O. Operators could not open an interactive shell from the WebUI, and directly exposing CubeMaster or Cubelet would bypass the existing CubeAPI authentication boundary.

This change keeps browsers on the same-origin CubeAPI surface. Session creation uses the existing HTTP authentication middleware, while the WebSocket URL contains only a short-lived, single-use grant rather than a long-lived API key or WebUI session token.

## Impact

Users can open independent interactive `/bin/sh` sessions for running sandbox containers from either WebUI entry point. Non-running sandboxes remain disabled, multi-container sandboxes expose a target selector, and idle or disconnected sessions clean up their containerd exec process.

The default terminal idle timeout is 1800 seconds and can be configured with `TERMINAL_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECS`.

title: feat(node): add node isolation via scheduling-disabled label
body:
## Summary

Add cordon/uncordon (node isolation) support to CubeMaster, allowing operators to mark a node as scheduling-disabled so new sandboxes are **not** assigned to it while existing sandboxes continue to run unaffected.

## Motivation

Operations teams need the ability to temporarily take a node out of the scheduling pool—for planned maintenance, draining before upgrades, or fencing a degraded node—without killing running workloads. This PR introduces a lightweight, label-based cordon mechanism that is:

- **Control-plane owned**: only the isolation API can set/clear the cordon label; Cubelet register and the generic label API are explicitly blocked from touching it.
- **Database-backed**: labels persist in `node_meta_registration.labels_json`, surviving CubeMaster restarts and replicas.
- **Fail-safe**: corrupt `labels_json` causes scheduling to fail **closed** (node treated as cordoned).
- **Concurrent-safe**: per-node mutex serialises label read-modify-write operations (register, admin labels, isolation) to prevent lost updates.

## Changes

### New CLI (`cubemastercli`)

```bash
# Cordon one or more nodes
cubemastercli node isolate <node-id> [node-id ...]

# Remove cordon
cubemastercli node unisolate <node-id> [node-id ...]

# List nodes (shows SCHEDULING_DISABLED column)
cubemastercli node list
```

### HTTP API (`/internal/meta`)

| Method | Path | Handler |
|--------|------|---------|
| `PUT` | `/internal/meta/nodes/{node_id}/isolation` | Cordon node |
| `DELETE` | `/internal/meta/nodes/{node_id}/isolation` | Remove cordon |

### Core Logic (`pkg/nodemeta/`)

- **`isolation.go`** (new) — `SetNodeSchedulingDisabled()` with per-node mutex, DB transaction, and localcache sync. `stripAndPreserveSchedulingLabel()` ensures Cubelet cannot overwrite/delete control-plane labels.
- **`service.go`** — Label read-modify-write operations (register, admin labels) are now serialised under `labelWriteLocks`. `reload()` / `applyReloadResult()` synchronises cordon state across replicas. `toSchedulerNode()` sets `schedulingDisabled` on scheduler-facing `Node` objects. `readLabelsJSONForUpdate()` returns `ErrLabelsJSONCorrupt` for corrupt JSON (fail-closed).

### Scheduler (`pkg/base/node/`, selector filters)

- **`node.go`** — `SchedulingDisabled()` / `SchedulingAllowed()` backed by `atomic.Bool`; custom `MarshalJSON`/`UnmarshalJSON` serialise the field. `Clone()` correctly snapshots the atomic flag.
- **`prefilter.go` / `backofffilter.go`** — Use `GetSchedulableNodesByInstanceType()` instead of `GetHealthyNodesByInstanceType()`, excluding cordoned nodes from the scheduling pool.
- **`sandbox_run.go`** — Final admission gate: before dispatching to Cubelet, `refreshAndAdmitHost()` re-reads the node from localcache and rejects if it is now cordoned (handles race between selector selection and Cubelet dispatch).

### Localcache (`pkg/localcache/`)

- **`export.go`** — New `GetSchedulableNodesByInstanceType()`; refactors `GetHealthyNodes*` to share `collectCacheNodes`/`collectClusterNodes` helpers with a `requireSchedulable` flag.
- **`node_cache.go`** — `updateNodeFromMetaData()` sets `SchedulingDisabled` on the cached node.

### Constants (`pkg/base/constants/`)

- `LabelSchedulingDisabled = "cube.cloud.tencentcloud.com/scheduling-disabled"` — reserved label key, owned by control plane.
- `LabelSchedulingDisabledValue = "true"` — canonical value.

### Tests

| File | Coverage |
|------|----------|
| `pkg/nodemeta/isolation_test.go` (new) | Cord/uncordon unit tests, label strip/preserve, clone/export, reload sync |
| `pkg/base/node/node_scheduling_test.go` (new) | SchedulingDisabled/SchedulingAllowed decode + MarshalJSON round-trip |
| `pkg/localcache/export_schedulable_test.go` (new) | Schedulable node collection with cordon filtering |

## Verification

Manually verified on a single-node staging cluster:

1. Created a code-interpreter template (`sandbox-code:latest`) ✅
2. Ran Python code execution (E2B SDK) ✅
3. `cubemastercli node isolate <id>` → `SCHEDULING_DISABLED: true` ✅
4. Sandbox creation blocked → `no more resource` ✅
5. `cubemastercli node unisolate <id>` → `SCHEDULING_DISABLED: false` ✅
6. Sandbox creation restored ✅

title: cubemaster(cli): support positional template-id in tpl info/delete/redo
body:
## Motivation

The `cubemastercli tpl` subcommands required `--template-id <id>` as a flag for every invocation. This contradicts the docker/kubectl convention where resource identifiers are positional arguments:

```bash
# What users instinctively type (docker/kubectl style):
cubemastercli tpl info tpl-abc123        # ← was rejected with "template-id is required"
cubemastercli tpl delete tpl-abc123
cubemastercli tpl redo tpl-abc123

# What they had to type instead:
cubemastercli tpl info --template-id tpl-abc123
```

This friction is a usability papercut — the codebase already had the correct pattern in `destroy` (positional `<sandbox-id>`) and `create`/`commit` (flag-fallback-to-positional), but the template commands did not follow it.

## Changes

### Code (`cubemaster:`)
- **New `resolveTemplateID(c)` helper** — checks `--template-id` flag first, falls back to the first positional arg (`c.Args().First()`), returns empty if neither is present.
- **`tpl info`** — accepts positional `<template-id>`, added `ArgsUsage`.
- **`tpl delete`** — accepts positional `<template-id>`, added `ArgsUsage`.
- **`tpl redo`** — accepts positional `<template-id>`, added `ArgsUsage`.
- **`tpl render`** — intentionally untouched. Its positional slot is already the file path, so `--template-id` is the correct interface there.

Backward compatibility: `--template-id` flag still works exactly as before and takes priority over the positional arg.

### Docs (`docs:`)
Updated all `tpl info` / `tpl delete` examples in EN + ZH to positional syntax, with backward-compat notes. `tpl render` examples left unchanged.

### Tests
4 unit tests for `resolveTemplateID`: flag-only, positional-only, flag-overrides-positional, empty.

## Verification

**Unit tests:** `go test -run TestResolveTemplateID ./cmd/cubemastercli/commands/cubebox/` → 4/4 PASS. Full package tests pass with no regressions.

**E2E on live PVM cluster** (cubemaster on `0.0.0.0:8089`, real templates):

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| `tpl info tpl-b394e8e5...` (positional) | ✅ Full metadata + replica table |
| `tpl info --template-id tpl-b394e8e5...` (flag) | ✅ Byte-identical to positional (except ephemeral requestID) |
| `tpl info tpl-b394e8e5... --json --include-request` | ✅ Includes `create_request` |
| `tpl info` (no args) | ✅ `template-id is required` |
| `tpl info tpl-doesnotexist` | ✅ `template not found` |
| `tpl redo tpl-b394e8e5... --detach` (positional) | ✅ Server accepted redo job, returned `job_id` |
| `tpl delete` / `tpl redo` (no args) | ✅ `template-id is required` |
| Help output for all three | ✅ Shows `<template-id>` in USAGE |

title: network-agent: Panic after Fatalf to prevent nil-pointer dereference
body:
CubeLog.Fatalf only logs at FATAL level without terminating the process, unlike the standard library log.Fatalf. This causes execution to continue past fatal errors, leading to nil-pointer dereferences when subsequent code uses uninitialized objects (svc, apiServer, grpcSrv, tapFDSrv).

Add panic(err) after each CubeLog.Fatalf call in main.go so the process exits immediately with the error value, preserving it for diagnosis.

title: [Feature Request] Support custom HTTP Host header when accessing sandbox services

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
## Problem / Motivation

Cube currently proxies HTTP requests from the public sandbox URL to services running inside the sandbox. In the current proxy path, the upstream request keeps the original external request host as the HTTP `Host` header.

This is not always compatible with applications running inside the sandbox.

Many web frameworks and applications use the HTTP `Host` header for:

- virtual-host routing
- CSRF / allowed-host validation
- redirect URL generation
- OAuth callback validation
- local development server checks
- multi-tenant app routing

For example, a user may access a sandbox service through a CubeProxy URL such as:

```http
https://<sandbox-id>-3000.cube.example.com/
```

But the application inside the sandbox may expect to receive:

```http
Host: localhost:3000
```

or:

```http
Host: my-app.example.com
```

To align with E2B behavior, Cube should support customizing the HTTP `Host` header that is forwarded to sandbox services.

This feature is about **inbound HTTP access to sandbox services through CubeProxy**. It is not about outbound network policy matching, DNS policy, or `rules.match.host`.

## Current State

Confirmed from the current codebase:

- CubeAPI already has a `network.maskRequestHost` field in the sandbox network config model.
- However, the sandbox creation path does not currently forward `maskRequestHost` into the CubeMaster network config.
- CubeMaster's current `CubeNetworkConfig` does not include a corresponding field.
- CubeProxy currently forwards the original request host to the sandbox backend, using the incoming request's host value.
- SDK support for this option is not currently exposed.

Therefore, `network.maskRequestHost` appears to be a partially-present / reserved API field today, but it is not fully wired through and should not be considered functional yet.

## Proposed Solution

Implement support for custom inbound HTTP `Host` header forwarding for sandbox service access.

The likely API field is the existing CubeAPI field:

```json
{
  "network": {
    "maskRequestHost": "localhost:3000"
  }
}
```

When `network.maskRequestHost` is set, CubeProxy should forward requests to the sandbox service with:

```http
Host: <maskRequestHost>
```

For example:

```json
{
  "templateID": "tpl_xxx",
  "network": {
    "maskRequestHost": "localhost:3000"
  }
}
```

Then a request from the user to:

```http
https://<sandbox-id>-3000.cube.example.com/
```

should reach the sandbox service with:

```http
Host: localhost:3000
```

If `network.maskRequestHost` is not set, Cube should preserve the current behavior for backward compatibility.

## Expected Behavior

- Users can configure the HTTP `Host` header that sandbox services receive.
- The configured host should apply to inbound HTTP requests proxied by CubeProxy to user-exposed sandbox ports.
- The feature should work for both host-based and path-based sandbox service access if both routes are supported.
- WebSocket upgrade requests should preserve the same custom `Host` behavior because they are HTTP requests before upgrade.
- The original public-facing host should still be available through forwarding headers where appropriate, for example `X-Forwarded-Host`, so applications can inspect the external host if needed.
- If `maskRequestHost` is not configured, existing behavior must remain unchanged.

## Non-Goals

- This is not an outbound network policy feature.
- This should not change DNS filtering behavior.
- This should not change `network.allowOut`, `network.denyOut`, or L7 egress `rules`.
- This should not affect CubeAPI management routes or internal control-plane traffic.
- This should not silently rewrite `Host` for sandboxes that did not opt into this behavior.

## API / Compatibility Notes

Use the existing `network.maskRequestHost` field if confirmed as the intended E2B-compatible field.

Open question:

- Confirm whether E2B's public API field name is exactly `maskRequestHost`.
- If E2B uses a different field name, Cube should either:
  - support that exact field name, or
  - support it as an alias while keeping `maskRequestHost` for backward compatibility.

Validation should reject invalid host header values.

At minimum, reject:

- empty string
- values containing CR/LF
- values containing URL scheme, path, query, or fragment
- malformed `host[:port]` values

Examples of valid values:

```text
localhost
localhost:3000
my-app.example.com
my-app.example.com:8080
127.0.0.1:3000
[::1]:3000
```

Examples of invalid values:

```text
https://example.com
example.com/path
example.com?x=1
bad-host\r\nInjected: value
```

## Implementation Notes

The implementation likely needs changes in the following areas:

1. CubeAPI

   - Keep accepting `network.maskRequestHost`.
   - Include it when building the CubeMaster-side network config.
   - Add validation before forwarding the request.
   - Avoid silently accepting the field if it cannot be applied.

2. CubeMaster

   - Add the corresponding field to the sandbox network config type.
   - Persist the value as part of sandbox proxy metadata.
   - Make it available to CubeProxy together with existing sandbox backend metadata.

3. CubeProxy

   - Load the configured custom request host from sandbox metadata.
   - If present, set the upstream HTTP `Host` header to that value.
   - If absent, keep the current behavior.
   - Ensure the behavior applies consistently to relevant sandbox service proxy routes.
   - Preserve original request host in forwarding headers where appropriate.

4. SDKs

   - Expose the option in supported SDKs.
   - Keep field naming aligned with the final API decision.

5. Tests

   Add coverage using a sandbox service that echoes the received HTTP headers.

   Test cases should include:

   - no `maskRequestHost`: service receives the current/default Host behavior
   - `maskRequestHost = "localhost:3000"`: service receives `Host: localhost:3000`
   - `maskRequestHost = "my-app.example.com"`: service receives `Host: my-app.example.com`
   - invalid host values are rejected at API validation time
   - WebSocket or HTTP upgrade path keeps the same Host behavior if applicable
   - both host-based and path-based proxy routes behave consistently if both are supported

## Acceptance Criteria

- A sandbox can be created with a custom inbound HTTP Host header setting.
- Requests routed through CubeProxy to sandbox services use the configured Host header.
- Existing sandboxes without this option continue to behave exactly as before.
- Invalid Host header values are rejected.
- The value is propagated through CubeAPI, CubeMaster, metadata storage, and CubeProxy.
- SDKs expose the option once the final field name is confirmed.
- Tests demonstrate the sandbox application can observe the configured Host header.

title: [Feature Request] Support runtime updates to sandbox network policy

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
## Problem / Motivation

Cube currently supports configuring sandbox network policy when creating a sandbox, but updating the network policy of an existing sandbox is not implemented yet.

This feature is needed to align with E2B-style sandbox behavior where network access can be changed during the sandbox lifecycle. Typical use cases include:

- Create a sandbox with broader network access for initialization, then restrict it after setup.
- Temporarily allow access to package mirrors, model endpoints, or external APIs for a specific task.
- Update domain/IP allow/deny rules without recreating the sandbox.
- Manage long-running sandboxes whose network permissions need to change over time.

Today, users have to recreate or clone a sandbox to apply a different network policy. That is heavier than necessary and may not preserve the same sandbox identity or runtime state.

This feature must also be designed carefully with the existing clone behavior in mind.

## Proposed Solution

Implement runtime network policy update support for an existing sandbox.

Proposed API:

```http
PUT /sandboxes/:sandboxID/network
```

The request body should reuse the existing sandbox creation API's network-related fields where possible.

Current confirmed request field behavior in CubeAPI:

- Top-level `allow_internet_access` is supported.
- Top-level `allowInternetAccess` is not currently supported by CubeAPI and should not be assumed unless we explicitly add it as part of this feature.
- Inside `network`:
  - `allowOut` is the canonical field name.
  - `allow_out` is also accepted as an input alias.
  - `denyOut` is the canonical field name.
  - `deny_out` is also accepted as an input alias.
  - `allowPublicTraffic`, `maskRequestHost`, and `rules` are part of the existing network config shape.

Example request:

```json
{
  "allow_internet_access": false,
  "network": {
    "allowOut": [
      "api.example.com",
      "1.2.3.4/32"
    ],
    "denyOut": [
      "0.0.0.0/0"
    ],
    "rules": [
      {
        "name": "deny-example-org",
        "match": {
          "host": "example.org",
          "sni": "example.org"
        },
        "action": {
          "allow": false,
          "audit": "metadata"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Expected behavior:

- Update the network policy of the target sandbox without recreating the sandbox.
- Apply the new policy to the sandbox's active network dataplane state.
- Replace the previous policy rather than appending duplicate stale entries.
- Reuse the same validation rules as sandbox creation where applicable.
- Return a clear error when the target sandbox does not exist or is not in a state that supports network update.
- Keep the API behavior compatible with E2B expectations, while preserving Cube's existing request field compatibility.

Validation should include existing network policy constraints, such as:

- Domain entries in `allowOut` / `allow_out` must follow the same deny-all requirement as sandbox creation.
- Invalid CIDR/domain/rule formats should be rejected before applying partial changes.
- A failed update should not leave the sandbox with a partially-applied policy.

## Clone Compatibility Requirements

The implementation must consider the existing clone behavior.

At minimum, the design should ensure:

- Updating the source sandbox's network policy after clone should not unexpectedly mutate the cloned sandbox's policy.
- Updating the cloned sandbox's network policy should not unexpectedly mutate the source sandbox's policy.
- If a cloned sandbox inherits the source sandbox's network policy, that policy should be treated as the clone's own effective policy after clone.
- Runtime network policy update should not introduce shared mutable policy state between source and clone.

Exact clone API behavior and whether clone should support an explicit network policy override should be confirmed during design/implementation. This issue does not assume that such an override already exists.

## Alternatives Considered

1. Recreate the sandbox with a new network policy.

   This is simple but loses the existing sandbox identity and may lose runtime state.

2. Clone the sandbox with a different network policy.

   This is still heavier than an in-place update and changes the sandbox ID. It also does not address the need to modify the original sandbox's policy.

3. Add a Cube-specific API only.

   This may be easier internally, but it does not satisfy the E2B alignment goal. The preferred approach is to implement the E2B-compatible API surface where possible.

## Additional Context

The CubeAPI README currently lists this endpoint as not implemented:

```http
PUT /sandboxes/:sandboxID/network
```

This issue tracks implementing that endpoint and wiring it through the required backend components.

Test coverage should include:

- Updating a running sandbox from internet access enabled to restricted egress.
- Updating a running sandbox from restricted egress to internet access enabled.
- Replacing `allowOut` / `denyOut` entries and verifying stale entries do not remain active.
- Replacing domain/L7 `rules` and verifying old rules no longer apply.
- Rejecting invalid update requests without partially applying them.
- Verifying source and cloned sandboxes can be updated independently after clone.

- Updating the source sandbox's network policy after clone should not unexpectedly mutate the cloned sandbox's policy.
- Updating the cloned sandbox's network policy should not unexpectedly mutate the source sandbox's policy.
- If a cloned sandbox inherits the source sandbox's network policy, that policy should be treated as the clone's own effective policy after clone.
- Runtime network policy update should not introduce shared mutable policy state between source and clone.

Exact clone API behavior and whether clone should support an explicit network policy override should be confirmed during design/implementation. This issue does not assume that such an override already exists.

## Alternatives Considered

1. Recreate the sandbox with a new network policy.

   This is simple but loses the existing sandbox identity and may lose runtime state.

2. Clone the sandbox with a different network policy.

   This is still heavier than an in-place update and changes the sandbox ID. It also does not address the need to modify the original sandbox's policy.

3. Add a Cube-specific API only.

   This may be easier internally, but it does not satisfy the E2B alignment goal. The preferred approach is to implement the E2B-compatible API surface where possible.

## Additional Context

The CubeAPI README currently lists this endpoint as not implemented:

```http
PUT /sandboxes/:sandboxID/network
```

This issue tracks implementing that endpoint and wiring it through the required backend components.

Test coverage should include:

- Updating a running sandbox from internet access enabled to restricted egress.
- Updating a running sandbox from restricted egress to internet access enabled.
- Replacing `allowOut` / `denyOut` entries and verifying stale entries do not remain active.
- Replacing domain/L7 `rules` and verifying old rules no longer apply.
- Rejecting invalid update requests without partially applying them.
- Verifying source and cloned sandboxes can be updated independently after clone.

## Summary

Build a first-class SDK compatibility E2E test framework for CubeSandbox, enabling the same user-facing scenarios to be validated across both the `cubesandbox` native Python SDK and `e2b`-compatible Python SDKs.

Resolves #864.

## Changes

### 1. SDK Compatibility E2E Framework

Added `tests/e2e/sdk_compat/` with a complete pytest-based framework:

- **Adapter layer** (`adapters/`): `SandboxAdapter` ABC with 16 backend-neutral methods. `CubeSandboxAdapter` and `E2BAdapter` wrap each SDK, normalizing return types and behavioral differences (e.g., E2B raises exceptions on non-zero exit codes vs CubeSandbox returns results).
- **Capability markers** (`framework/capabilities.py`): `requires_capability` marker auto-skips unsupported tests — E2B backend correctly skips `set_timeout`, `pause_resume`, and `proxy_url` with zero branching inside test bodies.
- **Preflight checks** (`framework/preflight.py`): session-scoped validation of CubeAPI health and template readiness, with early exit to avoid wasting resources.
- **Structured reporting** (`framework/reporting.py`): JSONL events for preflight, sandbox create/cleanup, and test results (backend, sandbox ID, duration, outcome, error diagnostics).
- **Safe cleanup** (`framework/cleanup.py`): `safe_kill` never raises — REST DELETE fallback, original test failure always preserved.

### 2. Nine Capability Domains, 44 Backend-Neutral Test Cases

| Domain | Tests | Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| lifecycle | 6 | create, info, kill, set_timeout, pause/resume |
| commands | 8 | stdout/stderr/exit_code, env, cwd, special chars, multiline/large output, missing binary |
| filesystem | 10 | read/write, overwrite, exists, list, make_dir, remove, nested dirs, cross-API interop |
| run_code | 8 | expression, stdout, kernel state, multiline blocks, string/list output, imports, error reporting |
| metadata | 2 | env var propagation, cross-API metadata interop |
| errors | 2 | info after kill, double-kill idempotency |
| concurrency | 2 | sequential reuse, parallel sandbox isolation |

title: [Bug Report] Native image export does not support HTTP (insecure) container registries
body:
## Summary

**Affected versions**: v0.5.0+ (introduced by PR [#558](https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/pull/558))

**Severity**: High

**Symptom**: When using an HTTP (non-TLS) container registry, CubeMaster template creation (`create-from-image`) fails with an error like:

```
native export failed to resolve image "my-registry:5000/my-image:tag"
  (if this is a multi-arch index, verify the requested platform exists):
GET https://my-registry:5000/v2/: dial tcp: ...
```

---

## Root Cause

PR [#558](https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/pull/558) introduced a pure-Go native image export that uses `go-containerregistry` to pull images directly, replacing docker/skopeo/umoci. The `go-containerregistry` library defaults to HTTPS, and the current code provides no way to mark a registry as HTTP (insecure).

**`CubeMaster/pkg/templatecenter/image/source.go:75-98` — `prepareNativeSource()`**:

```go
rawRef := strings.TrimPrefix(spec.ImageRef, "docker://")
ref, err := name.ParseReference(rawRef)   // No name.Insecure option
// ...
img, err := remote.Image(ref,             // Defaults to HTTPS; HTTP registries fail
    remote.WithContext(ctx), authOpt, platOpt, jobsOpt)
```

`go-containerregistry` requires passing `name.Insecure` to `name.ParseReference()` for HTTP registries. The current code neither passes this option nor provides any API parameter to control it.

---

## Why This Was Not a Problem Before

Before PR [#558](https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/pull/558), image pulling used either docker or skopeo+umoci paths, both of which handle HTTP registries natively:

| Export path | HTTP registry support | How |
|------------|----------------------|-----|
| Docker | ✅ | Docker daemon reads `insecure-registries` from `/etc/docker/daemon.json` |
| Dockerless (skopeo + umoci) | ✅ | skopeo reads system `registries.conf`, supports `insecure=true` |
| **Native (go-containerregistry)** | **❌** | `remote.Image()` defaults to HTTPS, no insecure entry point |

---

## Critical Detail: The Feature Is Enabled by Default

**`CubeMaster/pkg/templatecenter/image/native.go:44-47`**:

```go
func nativeRootfsExportEnabled() bool {
    v, err := strconv.ParseBool(os.Getenv("CUBEMASTER_NATIVE_ROOTFS_EXPORT_ENABLED"))
    return err != nil || v  // Returns true when unset → enabled by default
}
```

Native mode is **opt-out**. Users are automatically switched to the native path on upgrade, and HTTP registries break immediately. Only explicitly setting `CUBEMASTER_NATIVE_ROOTFS_EXPORT_ENABLED=false` can fall back to the old paths.

---

## Affected Code Paths

| Entry point | File | Line |
|------------|------|------|
| New template `create-from-image` | `image_job_runner.go` | L45 (constructs `SourceSpec`) |
| Template redo | `redo.go` | L243 (calls `PrepareLocalSource`) |

`PrepareLocalSource()` also uses `prepareNativeSource()` internally, so the redo path is equally affected.

---

## Scope of Impact

- Users with HTTP-only private registries (common in internal networks, offline deployments, image cache/proxy setups)
- Automatically affects all users upgrading to v0.5.0+ since native mode is enabled by default

---

## Workaround

Set `CUBEMASTER_NATIVE_ROOTFS_EXPORT_ENABLED=false` to fall back to the docker/skopeo paths.

---

## Related

- Introducing PR: [#558 feat(image): implement optimized pure-Go native image rootfs export](https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/pull/558)
- `go-containerregistry` version: `v0.21.6`

title: [Feature] SDK compatibility E2E test framework and quality gates

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
## Summary

Build a first-class SDK compatibility E2E test framework for CubeSandbox so the same user-facing scenarios can be validated across the CubeSandbox Python SDK and E2B-compatible Python SDKs.

The framework should provide stable PR-gate coverage, richer daily dual-SDK compatibility checks, and clear diagnostics for live environment, sandbox lifecycle, command execution, filesystem, code execution, network, proxy, and CubeSandbox-specific capabilities.

## Motivation / Use cases

CubeSandbox exposes both native SDK behavior and E2B-compatible SDK behavior. As these SDKs evolve, regressions can appear in only one backend or in shared platform behavior that is difficult to diagnose from API-level tests alone.

A dedicated SDK compatibility E2E framework is useful for:

* Validating that core SDK user flows work consistently across `cubesandbox` and `e2b` backends.
* Keeping PR-gate checks fast and stable by defaulting to the CubeSandbox SDK backend.
* Running broader dual-SDK compatibility checks in daily or weekly jobs.
* Detecting environment problems early through preflight checks before per-test sandboxes are created.
* Producing structured reports with backend, sandbox ID, duration, outcome, and failure context.
* Gradually expanding coverage from lifecycle, commands, filesystem, and run_code into network, proxy, metadata, errors, and concurrency domains.

## Proposal

Add and evolve an in-repository pytest-based framework under `tests/e2e/sdk_compat` with the following design:

* **Backend-neutral test cases**: keep cases organized by capability domain, for example `lifecycle`, `commands`, `filesystem`, `run_code`, `network`, `proxy`, `metadata`, `errors`, and `concurrency`.
* **SDK adapter layer**: expose a small shared surface over CubeSandbox SDK and E2B SDK behavior, including sandbox creation, info, commands, files, run_code, pause/resume, and future CubeSandbox-specific capabilities.
* **Capability markers**: use markers and capability flags so tests can express backend requirements without hard-coding backend branches in test bodies.
* **Default PR gate**: default live runs to `cubesandbox` backend only, while allowing `SDK_E2E_BACKENDS=e2b,cubesandbox` for daily dual-SDK compatibility.
* **Preflight checks**: validate CubeAPI health, template readiness, and required runtime features before creating per-test sandboxes.
* **Structured reporting**: write JSONL events for preflight, sandbox create/cleanup, test result, duration, backend, sandbox ID, and failure diagnostics.
* **Safe cleanup**: ensure per-test sandbox cleanup is best-effort and does not hide the original test failure, with room for orphan cleanup tooling.
* **Documentation**: document local setup, backend selection, TLS/CA handling, execution scopes, marker strategy, and expected reports.

## Goals

* Provide a reliable PR-gate suite for SDK compatibility using the CubeSandbox SDK backend by default.
* Support optional dual-SDK compatibility runs against both CubeSandbox SDK and E2B SDK.
* Make live environment failures easier to diagnose through preflight checks and structured reporting.
* Keep test cases scalable by organizing them by capability domain instead of large flat files.
* Reuse relevant coverage ideas from the existing `CubeSandboxTest` suite while keeping API contract, performance, resilience, CLI, Host Mount, Browser, and long-running tests in their specialized suites.
* Establish a clear roadmap for expanding SDK compatibility coverage from P0 smoke/core flows to P1/P2/P3 broader regression scenarios.

title: fix(cubemaster): sync timeout metadata after resume
body:
## Summary

`UpdateRequest` had no `timeout` field, so the timeout CubeAPI forwards with a
resume request was silently dropped — a resumed sandbox always kept its
pre-pause timeout. This PR carries it through, with regression tests and
lifecycle docs.

## Changes

- `types.UpdateRequest`: new optional `Timeout *int`; `nil` preserves the stored timeout.
- `Update()` (resume only):
  - rejects `timeout < -1` with `MasterParamsError` — same policy as `SetTimeout`
  - after a successful resume, publishes an explicit timeout to lifecycle metadata via `refreshTimeoutMeta`
  - best-effort by design: metadata failures are logged at error level and never alter the resume response
- CubeMaster unit tests for validation, `nil`/`0`/`-1`/`N`, success-only publish, and provider failure
- `sdk_compat` e2e: `resume(timeout=-1)`, `resume(timeout=-2)` → 400, `resume(timeout=0)` preserves TTL
- English and Chinese lifecycle docs: per-API timeout tables

## Behavior

| resume `timeout` | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| omitted / `nil` | dropped | preserve stored timeout |
| `0` | dropped | preserve stored timeout (immediate expiry is `set_timeout(0)`-only) |
| `-1` | dropped | never-timeout |
| `N > 0` | dropped | N-second window from now |
| `< -1` | dropped | `MasterParamsError` |

Publishing runs only after the resume RPC succeeds.

## Out of scope

This PR does **not** implement:

- refresh never-timeout / omitted-duration cluster default
- CubeAPI inbound `Validate` on `ResumedSandbox` / `ConnectSandbox`
- E2B `endAt` far-future sentinel

## Test plan

- [x] `go test -short -gcflags=all=-l ./pkg/service/sandbox/`
- [ ] `make cubemaster-test` / CI Unit Test Check
- [ ] `tests/e2e/sdk_compat/cases/lifecycle/test_resume_timeout.py` against a live cluster (`CUBE_TEMPLATE_ID` required)

## Motivation

The `AI Assistant / claude-response` workflow currently starts on ordinary PR comments and reviews even when CubeBot was not explicitly requested.

In those cases, `anthropics/claude-code-action` reports that no trigger phrase was found and can still fail during actor permission checks, creating false red checks on PRs.

## What Changed

* Add a job-level guard so `claude-response` only runs when the event body contains `/cubebot`.

## Scope

It does not change the existing `/cubebot` trigger phrase, and it does not add broader aliases such as `@cubebot`.

title: feat: add template-level ivshmem opt-in
body:
## Motivation

CubeSandbox already uses vsock for host/guest communication. That remains a good default abstraction for command, control, and general streaming use cases.

For performance-sensitive data paths, a shared-memory backend can provide better throughput and latency characteristics than a socket stream. `ivshmem` gives CubeSandbox a way to add that backend without changing the default communication path for existing templates.

This PR exposes `ivshmem` as an experimental, template-level opt-in. Keeping it template-scoped makes the capability explicit, avoids changing normal sandbox behavior, and keeps normal snapshot/restore flows unchanged unless the template has requested ivshmem support.

## What Changed

* Add template-level `enableIvshmem` support across CubeAPI, CubeMaster, cubemastercli, and the Python SDK.
* Persist the opt-in as an internal CubeMaster annotation.
* Have CubeShim create and clean up one host-side ivshmem backend file per sandbox:

  * `/dev/shm/ivshmem-{sandbox_id}`
* Retarget existing snapshot ivshmem devices to the new sandbox backend path during restore.
* Keep ivshmem disabled by default.
* Avoid injecting ivshmem into existing non-ivshmem templates or snapshots.
* Add public examples for host-side mmap benchmarking and minimal host/guest communication over an ivshmem-backed ring buffer.

## Validation

Focused tests:

```bash
cd CubeAPI && cargo test --locked services::templates::tests
cd CubeMaster && go test ./pkg/templatecenter ./cmd/cubemastercli/commands/cubebox ./pkg/service/sandbox/types
cd hypervisor && cargo test --locked update_ivshmem
cd CubeShim/shim && cargo test --locked ivshmem
```

The following validation was also run on a real verification server: Tencent Lighthouse, 4 vCPU, 8 GB memory, PVM enabled, Linux kernel `6.6.69-1.1.cubesandbox.oc9.x86_64`, AMD EPYC 7K62 CPU.

Guest-visible device and communication:

* Built an ivshmem-enabled template successfully.
* Verified the sandbox used `/dev/shm/ivshmem-{sandbox_id}` as the host backend path, with a 1 MiB backend file and `0600` permissions.
* Verified the shim process mapped the sandbox shm backend in `/proc/<pid>/maps`.
* Verified the guest enumerated the ivshmem PCI device as vendor/device `0x1af4/0x1110`.
* Verified guest `resource2` and `resource2_wc` were present.
* Verified `Host -> Guest` and `Guest -> Host` byte exchange through the guest `resource2` mapping.
* Verified `examples/ivshmem/ivshmem_ring_demo.py` passed host/guest communication.

Snapshot, clone, and rollback lifecycle:

* `create/delete`: shared-memory read/write succeeded, and `/dev/shm/ivshmem-{sandbox_id}` was cleaned up after delete.
* `pause/resume`: shared-memory read/write succeeded before pause and after resume.
* `snapshot/rollback`: shared-memory read/write succeeded before snapshot and after rollback.
* `commit+create`: the source sandbox and cloned sandbox used different ivshmem shm paths, and shared-memory read/write succeeded in both sandboxes.
* 5-round create/read-write/delete soak passed with shm cleanup after every round.
* 3 concurrent sandbox create/read-write/delete checks passed with independent shm cleanup.

Default behavior and non-opt-in regression:

* A normal non-ivshmem sandbox did not create an ivshmem shm file.
* A normal snapshot/restore regression preserved state and did not create an ivshmem shm file on the restored clone.
* Restore retargeting was verified only for snapshots that already contain an ivshmem device.

## Performance Check

The benchmark compared an ivshmem shared-memory ring buffer with a raw vsock stream on the same host. The guest side used a C helper for both paths.

These numbers are included as a sanity check for the experimental data path, not as a stable performance guarantee.

Benchmark | Direction | Workload / runs | ivshmem ring avg | raw vsock stream avg | Improvement
-- | -- | -- | -- | -- | --
Throughput | Host → Guest | 512 MiB total, 64 KiB chunks, 3 runs | 6123.90 MB/s | 612.88 MB/s | ~10.0×
Throughput | Guest → Host | 512 MiB total, 64 KiB chunks, 3 runs | 18418.13 MB/s | 606.07 MB/s | ~30.4×
Throughput | Host → Guest | 64 MiB total, 64 KiB chunks, 1 run | 8814.47 MB/s | 612.51 MB/s | ~14.4×
Throughput | Guest → Host | 64 MiB total, 64 KiB chunks, 1 run | 19931.80 MB/s | 835.03 MB/s | ~23.9×
Latency | 8 B sample | Collected in the 64 MiB one-off run | 0.73 μs/op | 97.71 μs/op | ~134× lower
Latency | 8 B sample | Collected in the 512 MiB one-off run | 4.70 μs/op | 88.76 μs/op | ~18.9× lower

The two latency rows are separate one-off samples collected by the same guest-C benchmark script in different throughput runs. They are not a 3-run latency average.

Additional smoke checks:

These Python-based E2E checks validate API wiring, sandbox lifecycle, shared-memory access, and cleanup behavior. They are not intended to represent the ivshmem data-path ceiling because the demo uses per-message acknowledgements, Python-side polling loops, `mmap.flush()` on each round, and Python payload generation and verification on both sides.

* Python E2E smoke benchmark, 64 KiB payload, 3 runs:
  * Host -> Guest stayed in the 13.08-14.06 MB/s range.
  * Guest -> Host stayed in the 3.93-4.10 MB/s range.
  * All sandboxes were deleted and shm files were cleaned.
* Python E2E smoke benchmark, 4 KiB payload, 3 concurrent runs:
  * 3/3 concurrent sandbox create/communication/delete runs passed.
  * shm files were cleaned after the runs.
* Host-only backend mmap benchmark:
  * 13067.18-18144.02 MB/s across 3 repeated runs.

## Scope

This PR adds experimental template-level ivshmem opt-in.

It intentionally does not:

* enable ivshmem by default
* replace the default stdio/vsock path
* change normal non-ivshmem sandbox creation
* change normal non-ivshmem snapshot/restore behavior
* inject ivshmem into existing non-ivshmem templates or snapshots

Restore-time ivshmem handling is limited to snapshots that already contain an ivshmem device. Existing non-ivshmem templates and snapshots keep their original behavior.

## Notes

The ivshmem backend file is sandbox-scoped and uses `/dev/shm/ivshmem-{sandbox_id}` on the host.

title: fix(cubemaster): rebuild stale rootfs artifacts
body:
## Summary

Fixes #852.

This change prevents CubeMaster from reusing a READY rootfs artifact record when the master-local ext4 file is stale or missing. Before reuse, CubeMaster performs a lightweight `stat` validation: the recorded path must exist, be a regular file, and match the stored size. If validation fails, the existing build path claims the artifact row and rebuilds it instead of distributing stale metadata to Cubelet.

The reuse path intentionally does not re-hash the ext4 file. SHA256 is still calculated when the artifact is built and retained in its metadata, while reuse validation avoids multi-gigabyte disk reads and request latency in persistent-storage deployments.

The same readiness and lightweight file validation applies to redo jobs resuming at the distribution or snapshot phase. After acquiring the per-artifact build lock, redo reloads the authoritative artifact row and uses that refreshed row for status, generated-request, and local-file validation as well as later generation and distribution. This prevents a redo waiting behind a concurrent rebuild from distributing a stale token or SHA. If the row disappears while redo waits for the lock, redo falls back to rebuild; other errors from the locked reload fail redo with their original cause instead of triggering an expensive rebuild.

Redo cleanup also uses the per-artifact build lock and rechecks the row so it cannot delete an artifact that a concurrent create has just rebuilt.

## Why

After a CubeMaster Pod restart with ephemeral local storage, the database can still contain READY artifact metadata while `/data/CubeMaster/storage/.../*.ext4` no longer exists. Reusing that stale metadata causes compute nodes to download invalid content and fail with a SHA256 mismatch. A lightweight local-file check detects the missing-file scenario from #852 without adding full-file hashing overhead to every deployment mode.

## Validation

- Squashed to one commit as requested; current signed head is `6135bf8deec043e20f2cd922172e1d7c9bb853d7`
- GitHub reports the PR mergeable against current `master` (`3c1c399b3bcc5dc1953e44025762eca4ca24c335`)
- Added a lock-ordering regression test that returns token A before the wait, commits token B while redo is blocked, then verifies both generated annotations and distribution use token B/SHA B
- Added a reload-error regression test that verifies transient database errors fail redo with their original cause and never enter artifact build preflight
- `gofmt` on the changed Go files
- `git diff --check`
- Linux/amd64 compilation of the full `./pkg/templatecenter` test package with Go 1.25.7
- Linux/arm64 compilation of the full `./pkg/templatecenter` test package with Go 1.25.7

title: [Feature Request] Decoupling of CubeAPI Operations Logic and Architecture Refactoring

body:
## Problem / Motivation

<!-- What problem does this solve? Who is affected and how?
     Describe the use case clearly. -->

CubeAPI is currently a Rust/Axum-based E2B-compatible sandbox API server that assumes two distinct responsibilities: the SDK API and the operations backend. Coexisting within the same process, port, and authentication system, these components have led to issues where stateful logic contaminates the stateless service, an excessive security attack surface, authentication model conflicts, and coupled deployment and scaling.

## Proposed Solution

<!-- Describe the feature or change you'd like to see.
     Include API changes, new config options, behavioral changes, etc. -->

Completely decouple the operations logic from CubeAPI into an independent Go service (CubeOps). CubeOps is exposed exclusively to the internal network and features an independent authentication mechanism. CubeAPI remains stateless and publicly accessible, retaining only the SDK / E2B compatible interfaces. All non-SDK and non-E2B compatible interfaces, except for those related to CubeSandbox SDK and E2B SDK, are migrated to CubeOps. The SDK interfaces in CubeAPI originally accessed by the WebUI are modified to retrieve data via a direct connection to CubeMaster.

title: [Feature] E2B-compatible persistent volumes with a customizable storage plugin framework

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
## Summary

Add support for persistent volumes so sandboxes can keep data across restarts and across instances, with a pluggable framework that lets operators back volumes by any storage system of their choice.

## Motivation / Use cases

E2B-compatible sandboxes are often ephemeral, but many workloads need to persist data beyond a single sandbox's lifetime, for example:

- Reusing large model weights or datasets across many sandboxes without re-downloading.
- Keeping a user's workspace/project files between sessions.
- Sharing the same dataset (read-only or read-write) across multiple sandboxes.

Today there is no first-class way to attach durable storage to a sandbox, and no standard way to integrate different storage backends.

## Proposal

- **E2B compatibility**: expose persistent storage through an API aligned with E2B (declare mounts on sandbox creation, plus a simple volume lifecycle: create / list / delete). Users and SDKs should not need to know how storage is implemented underneath.
- **Customizable plugin framework**: provide an extensible interface so operators can plug in their own storage backend (e.g. object storage, NFS, or a proprietary system) without changing the platform. The backend choice should be selectable per volume.
- **Safe lifecycle**: a volume that is still in use should not be deletable, so data cannot be removed out from under running sandboxes.

## Goals

- Sandboxes can mount durable volumes that survive restarts and are reusable across instances.
- Storage backends are pluggable and swappable by the operator.
- Volume management is safe (no deletion while in use) and transparent to end users/SDKs.

title: fix(build): switch CubeAPI Dockerfile to single-shot build with safety gates
body:
## Summary

Remove the dummy-main dependency-cache phase in `CubeAPI/Dockerfile` which can produce broken ~400KB empty binaries due to Cargo's mtime-based fingerprinting (see rust-lang/cargo#9312). Switch to a single-shot build that copies manifests and sources together in one step.

## Changes

- **Remove dependency-cache phase**: The dummy-main trick can leave stale cached artifacts when `COPY src/ src/` overwrites files with newer mtimes, causing Cargo to skip relinking and produce an empty binary.
- **Single-shot build**: Copy `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, `rust-toolchain.toml`, `build.rs`, and `src/` together, then run `cargo build` once.
- **Release metadata ARGs**: Add `CUBE_VERSION`, `CUBE_COMMIT`, `CUBE_BUILD_TIME` build args for CI injection via `build.rs`.
- **Post-build sanity gates**: Verify binary size > 5MB and run `--help` to catch broken artifacts before they reach the final image.

## Verification

The binary size check (>5MB) and `--help` invocation act as hard gates — a silently-broken empty binary will fail the build rather than being published.
